claims.text: Local compositional homogeneity governs the premelting and melting behavior of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Uniform atomic mixing produces a more uniform distribution of bond energies.
Uniform atomic mixing raises the onset temperatures of surface premelting and melting.
Local compositional segregation creates weakly bonded regions that initiate premelting at lower temperatures.
Rapid quenching can produce nanoparticles with maximal atomic-scale mixing and uniform composition.
Mild post-synthesis annealing promotes controlled local compositional segregation.
The proposed comparison holds nominal composition and particle-size distribution approximately constant while varying compositional homogeneity.
Local compositional distribution modulates the uniformity of bond strengths at both nanoparticle surfaces and in their bulk.
Localized weakly bonded regions in compositionally heterogeneous or phase-segregated particles act as nucleation sites for premelting.
Changing local binding energies changes the thermal energy required for premelting and melting.
Uniformly mixed nanoparticles will have higher premelting and melting onset temperatures than segregated nanoparticles under identical thermal conditions.
Differences in mixing state will produce shifts in DSC thermal events and differences in morphological evolution observed by in-situ TEM.
Rapidly mixed, compositionally homogeneous baseline nanoparticles will exhibit a higher and sharper melting transition.
The proposed mechanism should apply particularly to 5–20 nm high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles, where surface effects dominate.
High configurational entropy is critical to the proposed behavior in the stated nanoparticle regime.
The magnitude of the transition-temperature shift may depend on alloy system and degree of segregation.
Particle-size-distribution effects may also contribute to premelting and melting behavior.
A lack of a statistically significant lower premelting or melting onset in the segregated batch, or a lack of correlation between heterogeneity and melting behavior, would falsify the hypothesis.
